summary: Defines the Sunset HTTP response header field, which signals that a URI is likely to become unresponsive at a specified future time. It also defines a sunset link relation type for pointing to information about the retirement. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A sign on a web page saying 'this will close on this date', so people can plan ahead.

questions: how to announce api deprecation date
what is the sunset http header
subtitle: Announce when a web service or resource will shut down.

tldr.problem: Web APIs and services sometimes shut down or resources become unavailable, but clients often don't know when this will happen. Without advance notice, applications relying on them break without warning.
tldr.mechanism: The Sunset header lets a server send an HTTP response with a date and time when a resource will become unavailable, giving clients time to adapt. A companion link relation type can point to information about the shutdown.
tldr.outcome: Applications can detect the shutdown date, alert users or developers, migrate to alternatives, or make backup copies before the resource disappears.

facts.label: IANA status
facts.value: Registered in Permanent Message Header Field Names registry

today: RFC 8594 is an Informational RFC and is not obsoleted. The Sunset header field is registered in IANA's header field registry and is available for use in any HTTP application.

sections.title: Why Resources Have Expiration Dates
sections.content: Most web resources are meant to last indefinitely, but many do not. Shopping orders exist only until confirmed, APIs get deprecated, regulations require data to be deleted after a set time, and services migrate to new versions. In these cases, a resource will become unavailable at a known time in the future. The Sunset header field lets servers communicate that date to clients that are prepared to listen.
sections.plainLanguage: Websites sometimes have to close or move, like when a store changes location. It helps when they tell customers the closing date in advance.

sections.title: The Sunset Header Field
sections.content:
The Sunset response header field contains a single HTTP-date timestamp in RFC 7231 format. When a server includes it, the server is saying the resource is expected to become unresponsive at that date and time. For example: Sunset: Sat, 31 Dec 2018 23:59:59 GMT.

Clients SHOULD treat Sunset as a hint, not a guarantee. The resource might stay available past the date, or it might go away sooner. However, since the hint comes from the resource itself, it carries some credibility. After the Sunset time, clients should expect 4xx errors, redirects (3xx), or connection failures.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is just a message from the server saying 'I expect to stop working on this date'. It's helpful but not a cast-iron promise.

sections.title: When Sunset Is Useful
sections.content: The RFC describes several scenarios where Sunset helps. Temporary resources like pending shopping orders exist for a limited time by definition. Migration scenarios occur when a service is moving resources to new identities, and wants to warn clients before the original URI stops working. Retention and deletion happens when regulations require data to be kept for a period and then permanently deleted. And API deprecation occurs when an API version is being decommissioned in favor of a newer version.
sections.plainLanguage: It's useful when a server knows something will shut down: a temporary cart in a store, a website moving to a new address, data that needs to be deleted by law, or an old version of a service being retired.

sections.title: Sunset vs Caching
sections.content: The Sunset header serves a different purpose than HTTP caching headers. Caching is about reusing the representation of a resource, while Sunset is about when the resource itself will stop existing. They complement each other: the caching headers tell you when a cached copy is stale; Sunset tells you when the resource itself is ending. Applications like search engines should treat Sunset information separately from caching directives, using it to warn users that a resource may disappear, while still accounting for the fact that the resource may change in the meantime.
sections.plainLanguage: Cache headers are about 'this copy of the page is old', while Sunset is about 'the page itself is disappearing forever'.

sections.title: The Sunset Link Relation
sections.content: In addition to the header, RFC 8594 defines a sunset link relation type. A server can use it to point to another resource that provides more information about the retirement. That resource might explain the sunset policy (when and how resources will be retired), provide details about an upcoming sunset, or describe mitigation strategies (how to switch to a replacement service). The linked resource can be any media type and can be aimed at humans, machines, or both. It appears as a Link header or a link element in HTML: Link: <http://example.net/sunset-info>;rel="sunset";.
sections.plainLanguage: The link relation is a way to point to a web page that explains what's shutting down and why, so people know what to do about it.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Notes
sections.content: Publishing a Sunset date can leak information. For instance, if a registration resource announces its expiration date, that date itself is sensitive information, comparable to publishing the expiration date directly. The Sunset header should be treated as a resource hint indicating intent, not as a definitive prediction. The advertised date may be changed or withdrawn by the resource owner, or an intermediary may have inserted the header. Applications should never depend absolutely on the Sunset date; the real test is attempting to use the resource. When a sunset policy is linked via the link relation, clients should verify the information is authentic and accurate, and check that any migration rules only apply to resources within the policy's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Just because a server announces a shutdown date doesn't mean you should believe everything it says about it. Always double-check, especially if the server is giving instructions on where to go next.
